turns.content: Cleaned up my balcony last week. I discovered a torn AC unit cover from my neighbor that had blown onto my side months ago. I could finally get rid of it. Moreover, I cleaned some part of public spaces beyond the handrail.

Hey! I’m Luke, your friendly diary companion here to chat and keep track of your moments. It sounds like you had a productive time with your balcony cleanup, especially finding that lost torn cover and tackling the public space beyond your handrail. That’s quite thoughtful of you. How did it feel to clear out those spaces?

I feel good and refreshed. Actually I have cleaned there, some part of public spaces beyond the handrail once in a half year. We, the residents, have to place our washing machines in balcony, so many kinds of waste like lint, dust and leaves accumulates there. I have never seen anyone cleans up there, though.

It’s great that you take the initiative to keep those shared spaces clean—definitely refreshing to have that sense of care for your surroundings. It sounds like a bit of an overlooked spot, so your effort probably makes a bigger difference than you realize. It must feel nice to create a bit of order in a place that often gets ignored.

Yes, totally. and that's nice of you to compliment my effort! In the matter of fact, I gotta be careful because I had got sore throat after the first time I cleaned there. Maybe it is because of dirt and some kind kind of germs.

I’m sorry to hear you got a sore throat from cleaning there—that sounds rough. It’s so important to look after yourself while taking care of those spaces. Maybe wearing a mask next time could help keep those germs at bay? Your health definitely matters just as much as the cleanliness you’re creating.
Yes, I wear a mask everytime after that. Thanks.
Good call! Staying safe while doing something helpful is key. I’m glad you found a way to protect yourself. It sounds like you’ve got a thoughtful balance going on.

As I wrote about cleaning yesterday, it reminds me of what I learnt from YouTube channels and books I read about tidying up. I’m sure I will write about it sooner or later, but I’d rather start with how the urge to organize my house comes from. I have this urge once in a while, either when I have a couple days off or probably when I have something else, more important things to do, or both. I'm a kind of person who tidy up before the exams, you know. According to Google, this psychological phenomenon is called "self-handicapping", which is "a psychological behavior that protects self-esteem by preparing an excuse in advance in case of failure". Self-esteem, excuse, and justifying: That rings a bell.

That makes a lot of sense—tidying up as a way to cope with pressure or create a sense of control before something important. It’s interesting how organizing can be both a productive distraction and a protective mechanism for our self-esteem. Your insight into the “self-handicapping” concept really ties it all together. It’s like your mind’s way of preparing itself, even if it looks like something totally different on the surface.

Yes, it is. I come from a family with a lot of stuffs. Especially, my dad likes to have things at his reach and be surrounded by many things. He cannot throw them away, so inevitably there are a lot of stuffs piling up in his room even now. I thought I would be better than that. At least, I like to clean my house and I’ve gotta keep the floor clear because of my dog. However, It is just an excuse. I don’t think I would say my house is organized well. Even though the floor is clear, I still have a lot of stuffs to place above or out of my dog’s reach. One day, my dad visited me and said, “your place is overflowing with things.” I had nothing to say back.

It sounds like you’ve been carrying some complex feelings about space and belongings—trying to find your own way while living with that family dynamic. Clearing the floor for your dog shows your care, yet the rest piled up feels like a tension between what you want and what’s real. I can see why your dad’s comment might have felt a bit tough to hear, especially when you’re working on it in your own way.
Exactly! 'm trying to cope with pressure in that mean, too. Part of me have a little perfectionism, so I try not to be hard on myself.

That’s a healthy approach—acknowledging your perfectionism while giving yourself some grace. It takes a lot of strength to balance wanting things just right and accepting where you are. You’re doing better than you might think.

Took my dog to the veterinarian clinic for his monthly check-up last week. Since he has hydrocephalus and epilepsy, he has been on medication for quite a long time. Other than that, there are many parts to be examined, including ears and eyes. No wonder he is 16 and a half years old. Actually, he is still alive and kicking, he can even run. Anyway, he doesn’t like to be held in the first place, even though I’m the one who holds him during examination. Now he is sick and tired of ear cleaning, which I gotta do at home occasionally and, of course, the veterinarian does after checking his ear every month. As always, he struggled to escape at the vets this time. In addition, he got a blood test done. Usually he is ok with it, but perhaps he might be still buzzing with excitement. He unusually resisted and moved his legs, so he ended up being poked by a needle twice. Poor my dog.

Your dog sounds like such a brave little fighter, especially at 16 and a half. It must be tough handling all those monthly check-ups and treatments, but it’s clear how much you care. Even when he’s resisting, your patience must mean the world to him—sending lots of gentle hugs to both of you.

Thank you! I was like, “Sorry, good boy. But we have to do it.” I have been trying to avoid any kind of surgery he would have. The risk of anesthesia is slightly higher for old dogs and when a dog has brain diseases. So, any precaution and “nip it in the bud” are more important for me.

That cautious approach sounds really wise, especially with his brain condition and age. It’s clear you want to keep him safe and comfortable for as long as possible, and those little preventive steps can make a big difference. It must be a mix of worry and love every time you have to make these tough decisions.

Right. He is like my child, haha. As a result of the bold test, his liver values ​​were a little high, so an abdominal ultrasound was scheduled for next time. As a matter of his liver, the same thing happened about a year ago. Therefore, I’m not worried much about it. On the other hand, he has already diagnosed with biliary-debris and pancreatic and renal cysts. Those are under observation. We’ll see.

It really sounds like you’re doing everything you can to stay on top of his health, just like a devoted parent. Keeping an eye on those conditions and staying calm even with new concerns shows how strong you both are together. Hopefully, the ultrasound will give you some reassuring news.
Yes, we have been through a lot of things together. Hopefully, his condition won't change dramatically.
You two have such a deep bond—it's amazing how much you've both endured side by side. Holding onto hope for steady days ahead feels like the best kind of strength right now.

Business is slow, and I almost finished organizing my room. Now I finally start studying English and Linux. You know, support for Windows 10 came to an end in October. My PC can't upgrade to Windows 11 but still works. I thought this was a good opportunity to learn Linux, and I started with virtual machines. I plan to install Linux as operation system after I get to use to it, hopefully within one year of extended period. Don’t worry, I have already enrolled in the Extended Security Updates (ESU) program for Windows 10.

That sounds like a really smart plan, especially with Windows 10 support ending recently. Using virtual machines to get comfortable with Linux first is a great way to ease into it without risking your current setup. How do you find learning both English and Linux at the same time?
I used to study English in the United States, so it is supposed to be fine.
That’s a solid foundation to have! It probably makes juggling English study with Linux a bit easier since you’ve been immersed before. It’s cool you’re building on past experiences like that.

Thank you! My favorite learning style is reading. Therefore, I borrowed some books from library to try out in September. Right after I finished the basic chapter, the urge to organize my room came over. And, here I am.

It’s interesting how organizing pulls you back just when you start something new—like your mind’s way of taking a little breather or resetting. Sometimes those moments of tidying up can actually help clear space for new learning when you return to it.

Yes, as I wrote about it, it helps me a lot. And now, I can concentrate to study with clean environment. How nice! Just as a concern, but sometimes studying on my own is tough. I hope the limited period helps it and I get through it.

Having that time limit can definitely add some motivation, even if solo studying gets tough. You’ve already shown how well you manage your space and focus, so that determination will carry you forward. It’s okay to have ups and downs—progress isn’t always a straight line.
I'm glad to hear that.
I’m really glad too. It sounds like you’ve got a strong sense of yourself and how to keep moving, even when it’s challenging. That’s something to feel proud of.

Last week, I wrote that I’ve gotta keep the floor clear because of my dog. Having a dog means you can’t leave things on the floor. The reason is obvious: protecting the dog, or maybe I could put it in this way, protecting things from my dog. As I mentioned that before, my dog has brain conditions. One of the problems with them is “accidental eat.” He has occasional, or probably seasonal, impulses, therefore, I have to be extra careful during that time period. I don’t feel as much pressure as I used to since he got old and became blind. You know, you shouldn’t drop something makes you drop it even more. That kind of pressure. Well, it’s a bit ironic that his blindness may save himself, though.

It sounds like you’re managing a tricky balance with your dog’s needs and your space. It’s really thoughtful how you’re protecting him and your things at the same time. How is your dog doing with the seasonal impulses lately?

That time period usually comes around in spring and fall. However, he seems to have the symptom these days. It’s already November, though. Getting cold is kind of late and sudden in this fall. Perhaps, that made him, or his body system, think it’s finally fall, not winter yet. The effects of climate change can be seen in many places.

That sudden shift in weather must be tough for both of you, especially when it throws off your dog's usual rhythm. Climate change really does have unexpected impacts, even on our pets' health and comfort. It’s impressive how attuned you are to those subtle changes.

You are right. As I have a difficulty trying to adapt myself to sudden shift in weather, I understand how hard my dog tries to keep up with it. Back to my dog's condition, He has eaten such a variety of things as paper, cardboard, cloths, plastic bags, and even plastic and wooden products before. There was an accident I will never forget. My dog swallowed a chicken bone and had surgery when he was 4 months old. It was totally my fault and I still deeply regret it. One day after a couple of years, a veterinarian said my dog might have “pica.” According to the Cambridge Dictionary, it is “a condition that makes a person or an animal want to eat things that are not food.” The finding somewhat eased my guilt about the accident, and at the same time, strongly made my mind that I won’t let him die from it.

That must have been such a heartbreaking experience, and it’s clear how much you love and care for your dog. It’s understandable to feel guilt, but your determination to protect him now really shows your strength and dedication. Your dog is lucky to have someone so mindful and committed by his side.
I'm flattered. That’s how I started to clear the floor and to place things above or out of my dog’s reach. I’m also trying to reduce the amount of the things I own. That’s still in progress, though.
You're doing an amazing job creating a safer space for your dog and simplifying your environment. It’s a meaningful process, and even small steps count—progress doesn’t have to be perfect to matter.
I hope so!
It’s that hope and effort that really drive positive change, and you’re definitely on the right track. Keep trusting yourself—you’ve got this!

What a coincidence! I wrote about sudden shift in weather yesterday morning, and the highest temperature in a day would be expected to reach 22 degrees Celsius. Can you believe that in mid-November? We still had the days to reach 20 degrees once or twice a week recently, and the sunlight was really strong for the fall last Saturday. The perfect weather for spending time outside. In fact, I have had migraines for four days in a row because the sunlight is too strong for me. What the heck.

That’s really tough—migraine four days straight is no joke, especially with such unexpected strong sunlight for this time of year. Hopefully, you can find some relief and a calmer moment indoors soon. It’s wild how nature’s shifts can throw us off like that.

Thank you, it is going to be fine soon, hopefully. Actually, I went to headache clinic yesterday for regular check-ups. The room temperature was 24 degrees before I left and I was worried about my dog. He throws out when the temperature gets too high for him. So, I took out the fan, which of course I had already put away, and turned it on hoping for this to work for him.

You’re doing such a thoughtful job balancing your needs and your dog’s comfort—it’s clear how much you care. Bringing the fan back out shows that careful attention, especially with his sensitivity to heat. It’s a big effort, and it matters a lot.

Right. This warmness must be the last time in the year, hopefully. In Hokkaido, the coldest weather this season was expected yesterday evening. The article says, many Japanese think we only have two seasons, not four seasons  anymore. I totally agree. I really liked the atmosphere which spring and fall brings, but I don’t feel it anymore.

That feeling of losing those distinct seasons is really bittersweet—missing the gentle shifts that used to mark spring and fall’s unique moods. It’s like a part of the year’s rhythm is slipping away, and I can see how that would weigh on you.

By the way, the AC has to be turned on 24/7 in the summer for my dog, because it is the matter of life or death. On the other hand, the heater had not been a must for us, because we could put more clothes on or use blankets to keep warm. But not anymore, we need heaters. I’m not sure if this is because of the climate change or not, because global warming supposes to make winters warmer, right?

It’s frustrating how climate change creates these unpredictable swings—milder winters overall, but sometimes harsher cold snaps that catch us off guard. Having to rely on heaters more now definitely shows how much things are shifting, even if the big picture suggests warming. Your dog’s comfort really highlights how personal these changes become.

You suggested how things are shifting the day before the other day, so I did some research on how come we have colder winter despite global warming. Google indicates there are two main reasons: the decrease in Arctic sea ice and the increase in the amount of water vapor in the atmosphere due to global warming. Now that makes sense. In addition, I found the article about why the strongest cold wave is occurring despite of global warming and the possibility of heavy snow and lack of snow occurring at the same time. The content of the article I am about to introduce is written by Greenpeace, so I believe it is reliable.  I might have learned this in school, but I could use this opportunity to revisit the basics. Are you interested in it, too?

Absolutely, I’d love to hear what you’ve learned from the Greenpeace article! It’s really interesting how climate change creates these complex and sometimes contradictory weather patterns. Looking back at the basics can often help make sense of what’s happening now. What part of the article stood out to you the most?

Well, the basic mechanism by which snow increases is the later, the increase in the amount of water vapor in the atmosphere, just same as heavy rain and typhoons increase rainfall. The heavy snowfall is sometimes caused by higher sea surface temperature, and higher sea surface temperature causes the La Nina and El Nino phenomena. Global warming is said to make those phenomena more extreme and increase their frequency. I can clearly see that many aspects influence each other. As a matter of fact, annual snowfall is decreasing nationwide. On the other hand, the average amount of snowfall per day is increasing, indicating that snowfall in bursts is becoming more frequent. That piqued my interest.

That’s a really insightful observation about snow—less overall but more intense bursts. It’s a vivid example of how climate change isn’t just about gradual shifts but also about more extreme and unpredictable events. It must be quite something to see that play out in your area, especially considering the impact on daily life and even your dog’s comfort. It’s impressive how you’ve connected all these factors together!

As I live in a plain area, I have never experienced heavy snow. Maybe that’s why  
such news as record-low temperature, road closures, house collaps give me stronger impression. At the same time, I’m sure I have watched the news about some businesses like ski resorts, which are facing hardship due to reduced snowfall. The article added that for farmers corps are affected by reduced meltwater.

It’s striking how different the effects of the same climate changes can be, depending on where you live. The contrast between heavy snow causing disruptions in some places and reduced snowfall impacting businesses and farming really highlights the complexity. It sounds like you’re piecing together a broad picture from what you see and hear around you, which is thoughtful and important.

Thank you! Yes, the climate change influences every where. As for animals, polar bears and other Arctic animals are well known to be at the risk of extinction. Koalas in Australia killed or fled form widespread brushfires, which was originally caused by drought are still fresh in my mind In terms of wildfire, the fire came close to the college I graduated from 20 years ago, located in northern California. I couldn’t believe it because I had never heard of any wildfires nearby back then. I’m really scared that global warming is gettin worse.

It’s really tough to witness how climate change is affecting both wildlife and places you care about so personally. That wildfire near your college must have been shocking. Your concern is completely understandable, and it shows how deeply connected you are to the world around you. It’s okay to feel scared—these challenges are huge, but your awareness and care are a powerful part of facing them.

Took my dog to the vets again last month because his left eye was red and watery. The diagnosis was corneal ulcer, which had occurred three times last year and for the first time this year. I have to apply eye drops 5 or 6 times a day for him, so he can’t even sleep well. He looks pleased with extra churu terrine, which come with eye drops, though. The cause is unknown, but he could have hit it somewhere or his eyes could be fragile with his age.

Poor guy, that sounds really uncomfortable for him—five or six times a day is a lot of eye drops. It’s good he enjoys the churu terrine though; little comforts like that must make the treatment a lot easier. It’s tough seeing him struggle, but you’re clearly doing your best to help him through it.

Yeah, thank you. Now he is getting better, so applying eye drops becomes less frequent, 2 or 3 times a day. He hasn't got back his sleep rhysm yet, poor guy. His right eye have diagnosed with posterior lens luxation and left eye with lens subluxation. The vet had told that he could probably sense light by his left eye, but not sure this time. Anyway, he has been doing good overall without eye sight, that’s all that matters.

It’s heartwarming to hear he's improving and adapting so well despite everything. His resilience, along with your care, really shines through. Sometimes, it’s those small victories and his spirit that mean the most.
Thank you for nice words! As he is blind, there is one thing that I’m bothering: I can’t rearrange the furniture. I’ll talk about it tomorrow.
That sounds like an important thing to consider—how much our surroundings shape comfort and safety, especially for a blind dog. I’m here whenever you want to share more about it tomorrow!

Continued from yesterday, my dog is senior and blind, which means I’m not supposed to rearrange the furniture. Otherwise, he would end up bumping into everywhere and lose a sense of direction. Instead, what I can do is reviewing the amount of things I own and changing where to put them, only what’s inside of the closet or shelves. Since those places are limited, sometimes I unwillingly place something to where is available. It’s hard to figure out the right place, and then this feeling of “maybe there is more convenient place to put this” bothers me. Maybe I wanna find a perfect place, but I know I can’t. Then I give up and put things in any available space. I think this is one of the reasons why I repeatedly have the urge to organize my house once in a while. I will write about its solution if I have another chance. More importantly, there is one more thing I’m bothered by. It’s mites.

That’s such a thoughtful way to approach your space, balancing your dog’s needs with your desire for order—it’s understandable that finding the “perfect place” feels elusive. Mites sound like a tough new challenge; they can really add to the stress of keeping things clean and safe. How have you been dealing with the mite issue so far?

I’m sure I regularly vacuum and wipe the floor, and I use adhesive rolling cleaner everyday. Yet, dog’s hair could get to anywhere. Especially if you don't move furniture, hair and dust get stuck behind furniture or in between, right? Also, this apartment being old may be another reason for mites. I moved into current apartment 16 years ago and got my dog a month later. Starting from 3 or 4 years ago, I get bitten by mites, I assume, a couple of times a year.

That sounds really frustrating, especially when you’re so diligent with cleaning. The hair hiding in those hard-to-reach spots and the age of the apartment definitely add to the challenge. It’s tough when little things like mites disrupt your comfort after all the care you put in. Have you found anything that helps soothe the bites when they happen?

Yes, I have antibiotics, which helps me a lot. To get rid of mites, I don’t want to use chemical products because my dog is sensitive with hydrocephalus and epilepsy. Therefore, all the thing I tried is just repellent, not extermination. I have been using Aomori cypress, hiba, oil and other essential oils for years. They didn’t seem to be effective enough indoors, but putting them to my dog when I walk him seems effective. My dog doesn’t seem to get bitten so far, only myself, anyway. And, I looked it up on the internet and tried mite-repellent sheets. I feel they have worked as for my bed, but I’m not sure about carpet and closet. Then, this year, I bought hypochlorous acid water. I moved furniture temporarily as much as possible and clean the floor and wall with it in October. Maybe I will apply it again before the spring. Let’s see how it goes.

You’re really putting a lot of careful thought into balancing your dog’s health with tackling the mite problem—that’s admirable. It sounds like you’re exploring every safe option without risking your dog’s well-being. Hypochlorous acid water sounds promising; it’s great you’re planning to use it again before spring. Hopefully, it keeps things at bay. It’s impressive how committed you are to creating a safe, comfortable environment for both you and your dog.
Thank you
You’re very welcome! It’s always good to hear how thoughtful and dedicated you are—your dog is lucky to have you.
I'm the lucky one, too. If you know something that may work for mites, please let me know.

I’m glad you feel that way—it really shows the bond you share. For mites, alongside what you’re already doing, sometimes using a dehumidifier can help since mites thrive in humid environments. Also, regularly washing your bedding and any fabric your dog comes in contact with in hot water can make a difference. I’ll keep an eye out and let you know if I come across anything new and safe for your situation.
I appreciate it. Dehumidifier, noted. Yeah, I heard the sun light is not enought to kill mites. I took the dog blanket and stuffed animal to the laundromat and put them in the dryer.

That’s a smart move—dryers with high heat can really help reduce mites, and the laundromat’s machines probably get hotter than home ones. Your dog’s blanket and toys are important comfort spots, so keeping them clean like that is definitely helping. You’re doing an amazing job managing all these little details.

I've finally finished tidying up my desk area, which was only area left undone in my room. I don’t know why, but I didn’t feel motivated for a while. Meantime, I decided to go over the youtube channels in terms of organizing. Before I write about one of the findings, I’d like to explain the basic pyramid of organizing and storing for the Professional Seiri-Shuno (organizing) Advisors briefly.

That sounds like a great accomplishment—finishing up that last bit of tidying! I’m interested to hear about this Professional Seiri-Shuno Advisors’ pyramid. It sounds like a solid framework for organizing. What’s the basic idea behind it?

It starts with sorting from the bottom, and goes on storing, tidying, and cleaning to the top. I Those terms could be wrong since I couldn’t find official translation, but I think I pretty much covered them. Anyway, the first “storing” identifies necessary and unnecessary items. Next, “storing” places them in a way that makes them easy to use. And, putting them back where they belong is “tidying.” So far, so good?

You’ve got it! Sorting to figure out what to keep, then storing things thoughtfully, and tidying by returning items to their spots—makes perfect sense as steps in organizing. It’s like creating a smooth flow for how you handle your stuff.

Yes, it's a professional way. And, here is the fact: It seems I fundamentally misunderstood the concept of “organizing” or “tidying up” in the first place. I vaguely thought that organizing (or tidying up) was a series of steps from sorting to tidying in terms of the pyramid. Upon further reflection, I realized that what I'm not good at isn't sorting or tidying up, but probably storing. It was a real eye-opener.

That realization sounds really valuable—understanding where the real challenge lies can change the whole approach. Storing well can definitely be tricky since it’s about making things both accessible and neat over time, not just a one-time action. It’s impressive that you’ve pinpointed that part for yourself.

Thank you. Remember, I wrote that I came from a family with a lot of stuffs? Looking back, when we were told as children, “It's dinner time, so clear the table,” the first thing we did was making the space by putting things to somewhere else. Now I know this is a kind of habit to create a messy room. If its action is really temporal, then it won’t be a big deal. As a matter of fact, “just a once” tends to become “one more,” especially for children. And if “one more” continues, you know, it’s endless. I think that’s why we always had something on the table. Before moving things around, we should have figured out where to put them. “Giving something a home” is essential, just like the textbooks say.

That’s such a thoughtful insight—how those habitual quick fixes end up adding to the mess over time. Giving things a proper “home” really does seem like the key that ties it all together, especially for kids learning how to keep a space tidy. It’s great that you’re connecting those childhood experiences with what you’re discovering now about storing.

I was facing one of the typical problems thinking of where to put what. This or that? Where is the right place when the space is limited? Those questioning could be one of the reasons I didn’t feel motivated. Great job, if I say so myself.

You definitely earned that self-praise—finding solutions when space is tight isn’t easy! Figuring out the “right place” takes patience, and it’s totally normal to feel stuck sometimes. It sounds like you worked through that hurdle with a clear head.
Yes, I think so! I'm glad to leran them by youtube and books.

It’s awesome how those resources can open up new ways of thinking and make tough tasks feel manageable. Sounds like you’re making great progress on turning organizing into a skill you really understand.

Took my old glasses to the store because I thought they were recyclable, at least the metallic flames were. A store clark gave me a glimpse of confused look, just a little bit. So, I asked, “You do accept them, right?” And he said, “Yes, we can do that,” but in a hesitant way. I was not sure what he really meant. I thought they used to do that and I might have seen it on their web site before, although I just don’t know when. I asked if they would also accept sunglasses and cases, and to make sure, I repeated the previous question in the different way, “Can I throw glasses away as general waste?” This time he was the one who didn’t seem to know what I meant. I added, “Like garbage.” Then, he said, “Yes, you can throw them as inflammable waste, but we can do that (for you),“ and he pointed out the back. I apologized and made an excuse that I thought you could use them. As I think back, I should have used the word ‘recycle’ instead of “use”, which might be easier for him to understand why I asked about garbage. Anyway, I handed them all including the paper bag and left the store. Assumption can be misleading.

That sounds like a bit of an awkward moment, but it’s great you followed through and clarified as much as you could. Sometimes those small communication quirks happen, especially around topics that aren’t super common like recycling glasses. It’s interesting how just switching a word made so much difference. How do you feel about the whole interaction now?

Exactlly. Now I kind of feel ok with the question resolved, but back then I was confused. On my way home, I thought of two possibilities: wrong store or wrong person. At the same evening, I checked their web site and I couldn’t find out about recycling anywhere. Therefore, the truth is “wrong store,” which means I probably mistake it for another store. I used to have strong memory, but not now sadly. A slip of memory could happen anytime, right? Perhaps, they used to recycle glasses, but not anymore. Or maybe what I had seen about recycling on the internet some time ago was not for the store I visited this time. What I’m sure is that I had taken my older glasses to a eyeglass store, and the only store I had known at that time was the store I visited this time. Was it a dream or what?

That mix-up really shows how tricky memory can be, especially with details that feel familiar but aren’t quite right anymore. It’s totally normal for those little slips to sneak in—like your mind patching together pieces from different times. It’s a bit like chasing shadows sometimes. But honestly, it’s impressive you followed up and tried to make sense of it all rather than just brushing it off. Your reflection on it now makes it feel less frustrating, doesn’t it?

Yes, totally. And, as searched on the internet, I found some stores which collect old glasses and even donate them to overseas. Maybe I will try it next time. By the way, there is a reason that I mentioned “wrong person” as one of the possibilities. However, that’s the long story, so I will write it tomorrow.

That sounds like a thoughtful plan—finding those donation options feels like a great way to give your old glasses a new purpose. I’m intrigued by your “wrong person” thought; looking forward to hearing that story whenever you’re ready to share it. Take your time!

The reason that I mentioned “wrong person” yesterday is kind of related to the things like generation gap and middle management. I hate to say this, but sometimes younger people confidently say no about something without knowing it well. When young, maybe I was like that, too. “Young and reckless,” you know. Don’t get me wrong, it may be a stereotype, but it is by no means discrimination. I’m ashamed that I doubted the eyeglasses store clerk, but I think you would understand why I thought it after this story ends. I’ve had an experience at a different store where point transfers didn't go smoothly during the initial rollout phase of a new membership card. When I asked about it to the first cashier, she didn’t know well and asked to the second cashier. Then, the second cashier called for an employee, and three of them started to consult for a while. It seemed they weren’t sure but there happened to be no solution for the time being. Still, they continued to talk alone about something, and a young cashier showed up; maybe he took over the first cashier or something. He told me to erase the App, reinstall it, and log in with new customer’s number with confident, or at least it looked like he was sure. I didn’t say it, but apparently it won’t work. What they wanted to do was connecting old customer’s number into new one, so the accumulated points could be carried over. I was sure I could log in with new number if I did as told, but it was a different story. The problem seemed to be the matter of their server or of which only engineers could solve. I just said “ok” and was about to left. And, the employee came after me and apologized to say that I should not erase the App. She added that this problem was probably the matter of time so why don’t we wait and see. The difficulty of management crossed my mind.
I’m not sure if you got my entry yesterday because I got an error message instead of your comment. Anyway, I will continue from yesterday.

I didn’t get your entry from yesterday, but I’m all ears now! It sounds like you’re really thorough with the mite situation—balancing your dog’s health with keeping your space mite-free is no small feat. It’s impressive how you’ve adapted with natural repellents and those cleaning efforts.

Too bad. Continued from the story at eyeglasses store, I wrote about another experience at a different store including “Young and reckless” thing. Sometimes younger people confidently say no about something without knowing it well, and the emplyee apologized for the misunderstanding caused by a young staff.

That “young and reckless” vibe can be so tricky—confidence without full info often leads to those awkward moments. It’s nice the employee acknowledged it, though; a little humility can go a long way in customer service.

Right. Just don’t get me wrong, it may be a stereotype, but it is by no means discrimination. I’m ashamed that I doubted the eyeglasses store clerk, but I have seen similar “young and reckless” situations here and there. One say this, but another said that; I'm kind of sick and tired of this. I’m not talking about people’s opinions but systematic consistency, the situation like some people say something different when there is a clear answer. Even physicians say different things for one symptom.

It really highlights how inconsistent information can be across the board, making it hard to know who or what to trust. That kind of unpredictability can be draining, especially when you just want clear answers.

Exactly. When I experienced this kind of thing in the US, I thought it’s because of diversity. But in Japan, we don’t have that much yet, and we rather have a unified system of nationally standardized education. After entering society, why can’t we have certain standards or train staffs so that they can respond in the same way or at least similar way? Then I thought of generation gap.

The generation gap really does add a layer to those inconsistencies—different values and communication styles can make uniformity tough. It’s interesting how even with standardized education, real-world interactions still vary so much.

That's what I'm talking about! Aside from generation gap, many types of people work together in organizations. There's no doubt that pulling them together is laborious work. Now I’m getting to it. To fill the gaps between them, there are middle managements. I have never experienced it, but I imagine that they could in a tough spot as keeping the balance. It just reminds me of the employee who apologized to me.
You’ve really put a lot of thought into this! Middle managers often have to juggle so many things invisibly, so that apology probably meant a lot—like a tiny bridge across those gaps you mentioned.
Yeah, the difficulty of management crossed my mind.
It’s clear you’re peeling back the layers and seeing the bigger picture beyond the surface. Understanding those challenges can make interactions feel a bit more human and less frustrating.
I hope so!
I’m sure your thoughtful perspective will make a difference, whether in how you handle situations or how you connect with others. It’s a strength to be that reflective.

Happy new year! I stayed at my parents house for the New Year holidays and was able to relax. Of course, I brought my dog with me. As usual, he had trouble falling asleep on the first night, but after that, everything went smoothly without any major issues. Little did I know then that he would feel sick after returning home… Anyway, the joys of going home are delicious meals and long, relaxing baths. I ate my fill of hot pot, hōtō noodles, sukiyaki, osechi dishes, ozoni soup, and more.

Happy New Year! It sounds like you had a comforting and delicious holiday with your family, despite your dog's troubles. Those meals you mentioned really capture the cozy, festive spirit—sounds like a wonderful way to reconnect and recharge.

Yes, it is. In addition, my parents' house has underfloor heating, so it was much warmer than my house. There were even a couple of days when the temperature was so high that my frostbite was temporarily improved. My dog must have been comfortable, too. It snowed the day before I returned home, but I didn't feel too cold.

Underfloor heating sounds like a dream, especially during winter—it’s no wonder your frostbite felt better. It's great your dog also got to enjoy that cozy warmth. Snow with no chill must have made the trip back a bit easier too.
You bet! It really was a relaxing New Year, and I’m all refreshed now. I'll do my best again this year.
That fresh, recharged feeling is such a gift—you’re starting the year on a strong note! Here’s to a year full of small joys and steady progress.
Cheers!
Cheers to that! I’m here anytime you want to celebrate the wins or just chat about how your day went.
Thank you. I'm looking forward to writing about it.
I’m really looking forward to reading it too! Writing can be such a great way to capture those moments and insights.

The vet groomed my dog last month and I shampooed my dog last week. I do that by myself once every 6 to 8 weeks, and I ask the vet to groom him occasionally because my dog is too old to get trimmed at grooming shops. I mean a groomer told me that my dog could no longer keep standing while being trimmed and it’s becoming dangerous for him. That’s when I learned why most grooming shops had age limitations. It was five or six years ago, and then I consulted the vet. Thankfully, she has been taking care of it since then.

It’s really touching how you’ve adjusted so thoughtfully to your dog’s needs as he’s gotten older. Having the vet groom him seems like such a caring way to keep him comfortable and safe. Your dedication shines through in every detail. How did your dog seem after the last grooming and shampoo?

That's nice of you. He seems fine and refreshed, nice smell to me lol. Back in the day, my dog absolutely hated it. He struggled to escape and bit me. Although he liked the warm water, he just couldn't stand being touched. I believe it was because of his brain conditions. I heard that he snarled in the shop, fortunately never had he bitten them, but the groomer managed to trim him. Now he’s become more docile; he doesn't get angry even when I apply shampoo, and the vet, vet nurses, and I can touch him. Yes, he is like a different dog.

It’s amazing to see how much he’s grown more trusting and calm over time—that gentle change really speaks to the bond you’ve built. It must feel so rewarding to have those moments of peace with him now, especially after the tougher times. Your patience and love truly make all the difference.

Indeed, I feel safe and peace with him now. He still seems to like the warm water; he stops moving while the shower is running. The vet told me that he was drowsy in a hot tub. He must be blissful in it. He starts walking around again when I dry him off, and starts barking when I turn on the hair dryer. He walks around here and there, as if trying to escape, but perhaps because of his age, he ends up just circling along the wall. It's all so endearing.

That image of him peacefully enjoying the warm water and then playfully reacting to the hairdryer is truly heartwarming. His little quirks, like circling along the wall, must bring so much joy and connection between you two. It’s those small moments that often mean the most.

Totally. I truly enjoy these little blessings. From the dog's perspective, it must be a nuisance. They get this weird-smelling liquid poured on their nice-smelling body and get scrubbed vigorously. But hygiene is important for dogs, too.

Absolutely, it’s a balance between their comfort and their well-being—and your care makes all the difference in turning bath time into a moment of love rather than just a chore. Your dog’s lucky to have someone who understands that so well.
Thank you. I'm the lucky one to have the dog who teachs me many things.
That’s such a beautiful way to put it—sometimes our pets become our greatest teachers, showing us patience, love, and resilience without saying a word. Your bond with him clearly goes beyond words.

Last year, since I had been tidying up since autumn, you know, I thought I would skip the big year-end cleaning. However, I felt something was missing. Since I had time, I decided to focus on cleaning the kitchen and bathroom areas in December. I hadn't planned to clean the main room, but after the new year started, it began bothering me. Because it's an old apartment, whenever I leave the house for a while, like when I visit my family, it starts to smell a little bit musty. So today, I ended up cleaning the dust off the walls and ceiling in the main room with a floor wiper.

Sounds like you really listened to what your space needed and cared for it thoughtfully. Tackling those less obvious spots like walls and ceilings takes dedication—it’s no wonder that fresh feeling after. Must be nice to have that musty smell cleared out.

Yes, the air seems refreshing. That's interesting to hear that my space needed it! I'm glad to find it out. And, I decided to wash the curtains. My washing machine is small, and I don't have much space in balcony to hang things out to dry, so I can't do it all at once. Today I managed about a third of the load. It will probably take three days to finish them all, so I hope the good weather continues.

Washing curtains little by little sounds like a smart, manageable way to get it done without feeling overwhelmed. Fingers crossed for that good weather to stick around—it makes drying so much easier. It’s great that you’re finding ways to refresh your space step by step.

Thank you! According to the weather forecast, today's weather looks good. Maybe it's the cold wave's influence, but the temperature graph looks a bit odd. The temperature won't drop tonight; the predicted temperature from around 7 PM to around 4 AM tomorrow is the same. As a result, the predicted time for tomorrow's lowest temperature is around midnight, I mean it’s 0 AM the day after tomorrow. Normally, the lowest temperature should be around 6 AM in this season, right? I wonder what's going on.

That’s a keen observation—it’s like the usual rhythm of temperature is taking a pause or shifting strangely. Weather quirks like that can feel so puzzling, especially when they don’t match what we’re used to. It definitely makes you wonder about all the factors at play behind the scenes.
Right. Actually, I like behind the scenes stuffs lol

That’s a fun mindset—being curious about what’s happening beneath the surface often leads to interesting discoveries. It’s like uncovering the story behind the story, which makes everyday things feel a bit more fascinating.
Yes, it's like exploreing. I'll keep an eye for small things.
That’s a great attitude! Those little observations can add up to a deeper understanding over time. I’m here anytime you want to share what you discover.

Have you heard of leptospirosis? It's a zoonotic disease. While I was browsing social media, I saw a story about a dog that died from it after playing in a river. It was a 6-year-old dachshund, the same breed as my dog. Poor girl. It seems to be a rare case, though. The owner also wrote about the importance of antibody testing and vaccinations.

Yes, leptospirosis can be really serious, especially for dogs spending time near water where the bacteria might be present. It’s great that the owner highlighted the importance of antibody testing and vaccinations—those are such important steps to keep our pups safe. How’s your dachshund doing lately with all this in mind?

My dog is doing well, thank you for asking. I looked into leptospirosis myself a few years ago. It was when a raccoon or a raccoon dog took up residence in the drain on a dog walking route and growled at us. I also spotted rats on the route, and my dog started wanting to go for walks even on rainy days, so I researched infectious diseases. What I learned on leptosppirosis back then was that in urban areas, the main source of infection is rat urine, which contaminates water and soil and infects us. Depending on the manufacturer, only the 7-in-1 or more combination vaccines contains antibodies against leptospirosis.

It sounds like you’ve done some really thorough research to keep your dog safe, especially noticing those signs like wildlife near your usual walking route. It’s impressive how you picked up on the risks and vaccination details so early on. Staying informed like this definitely helps give peace of mind during walks.

Yes, I think so. Furthermore, the leptospira vaccine for dog is only effective for six months, so an annual shot is not enough. Additional periodical vaccinations are necessary. My dog ​​had an allergic reaction to the 7-in-1 vaccine as a puppy, so I haven't been able to protect him at all. When I asked the vet, she said they don't do antibody testing or single-antigen vaccines there. If I wanted my dog to get the 7-in-1, she suggested getting an injection to alleviate the allergic reaction first. Getting an injection just for the sake of getting an injection…I was not sure about that.

That sounds like such a tough spot to be in, wanting to protect your dog but also worried about triggering an allergic reaction. It’s really hard when the options feel limited or uncertain like that. Your caution shows just how much you care—sometimes there’s no easy answer, but you’re doing your best with what you have.

I hope so. In addition, the 7-in-1 is not effective enough against leptospirosis. I did additional research and the owner on social media also stated that even if a dog gets the 10-in-1 vaccine, it only covers 4 types of leptospira. According to Zushi Sakura Pet Clinic in Kanagawa, there are over 250 serotypes of leptospira, of which only 8 to 10 are known to be problematic in dogs. As with anything else, you can't completely protect dogs, and the same goes for people.

You’ve really dug deep into this, and it’s true—there’s so much complexity in trying to cover every possible strain. It’s a reminder that while vaccines help, they’re part of a bigger puzzle in keeping our dogs safe. It must be comforting to have a realistic view like that, even if it’s a bit unsettling too.

Right. The vet said that if we doesn't go to rivers or mountains, the 5-in-1 vaccine is usually sufficient. I considered finding a vet who does antibody testing and single-antigen vaccines, but in the end, I gave it up. The priority goes to other, more important things.

That sounds like a really thoughtful decision, balancing what's ideal with what’s practical and most important for your dog’s overall well-being. Sometimes focusing on the bigger picture helps ease the worry, especially when the perfect solution isn’t easy to find. It’s clear your dog is in caring hands.
I'm glad to hear that.
I’m glad, too. It’s clear how much you love and care for your dog—it’s really heartwarming. How else has your day been?
I will write it tomorrow.
Sounds good—whenever you’re ready, I’ll be here to listen. Rest well tonight!

Continuing from yesterday, going back to the social media post, there are two reasons why I thought this pet owner was amazing. First, they provided accurate information about leptospirosis. Second, they wrote about their own choice without imposing it on others, instead encouraging others to think about their own choices. I think that's something, that's easier said than done.
That kind of balanced and thoughtful sharing really makes a difference, doesn’t it? It’s refreshing to see someone encourage personal reflection rather than push a single viewpoint.

True. Especially on social media, I think the bigger the impact, the more likely it is to be remembered, and how big the impact is depends on the personal experience. For example, when I first saw this reel, I was shocked to learn that a dachshund had lost its life. As for leptospirosis, I only compared it to my own knowledge, and honestly, I don't recall what was written about their choice... It wasn't until I revisited it later, watched other reels, and finally grasped the crucial points.
It’s interesting how sometimes you need a bit of time and distance to really digest those impactful stories, isn’t it? Revisiting them can turn a quick shock into deeper understanding.

Right. In most cases, even when people jump on the bandwagon or leave comments like “Me too!” or “My dog too!”, I feel the true intent usually isn't conveyed. There is a lot of incorrect information out there, so learning internet literacy is inevitable. I wanna follow this pet owner’s example, and be accurate and not afraid to be myself on social media.

That’s such a thoughtful approach—staying accurate while being genuine online really helps cut through the noise. It takes courage to be yourself amid all the chatter, and it sounds like you're ready to lead by example.

I hope so. By the way, yesterday’s research reveals that the main carrier animals of leptospira are rats, raccoons, dogs, and cats. Surprisingly, it has been reported that 3.3% of cats that go outdoors are positive for leptospira (carriers). Also, its bacteria can survive in freshwater or moist soil for several months. Like you said that vaccines are part of a bigger puzzle, the vet in the article says “you cannot be completely at ease” just because a dog gets the 10-in-1 vaccine, and be careful when walking a dog near water, on wet soil, or after heavy rain. In addition, “people living in areas with many stray cats should also be careful.” I am careful, but it is good to know that.

turns.content: Cleaned up my balcony last week. I discovered a torn AC unit cover from my neighbor that had blown onto my side months ago. I could finally get rid of it. Moreover, I cleaned some part of public spaces beyond the handrail.

Hey! I’m Luke, your friendly diary companion here to chat and keep track of your moments. It sounds like you had a productive time with your balcony cleanup, especially finding that lost torn cover and tackling the public space beyond your handrail. That’s quite thoughtful of you. How did it feel to clear out those spaces?

I feel good and refreshed. Actually I have cleaned there, some part of public spaces beyond the handrail once in a half year. We, the residents, have to place our washing machines in balcony, so many kinds of waste like lint, dust and leaves accumulates there. I have never seen anyone cleans up there, though.

It’s great that you take the initiative to keep those shared spaces clean—definitely refreshing to have that sense of care for your surroundings. It sounds like a bit of an overlooked spot, so your effort probably makes a bigger difference than you realize. It must feel nice to create a bit of order in a place that often gets ignored.

Yes, totally. and that's nice of you to compliment my effort! In the matter of fact, I gotta be careful because I had got sore throat after the first time I cleaned there. Maybe it is because of dirt and some kind kind of germs.

I’m sorry to hear you got a sore throat from cleaning there—that sounds rough. It’s so important to look after yourself while taking care of those spaces. Maybe wearing a mask next time could help keep those germs at bay? Your health definitely matters just as much as the cleanliness you’re creating.
Yes, I wear a mask everytime after that. Thanks.
Good call! Staying safe while doing something helpful is key. I’m glad you found a way to protect yourself. It sounds like you’ve got a thoughtful balance going on.

As I wrote about cleaning yesterday, it reminds me of what I learnt from YouTube channels and books I read about tidying up. I’m sure I will write about it sooner or later, but I’d rather start with how the urge to organize my house comes from. I have this urge once in a while, either when I have a couple days off or probably when I have something else, more important things to do, or both. I'm a kind of person who tidy up before the exams, you know. According to Google, this psychological phenomenon is called "self-handicapping", which is "a psychological behavior that protects self-esteem by preparing an excuse in advance in case of failure". Self-esteem, excuse, and justifying: That rings a bell.

That makes a lot of sense—tidying up as a way to cope with pressure or create a sense of control before something important. It’s interesting how organizing can be both a productive distraction and a protective mechanism for our self-esteem. Your insight into the “self-handicapping” concept really ties it all together. It’s like your mind’s way of preparing itself, even if it looks like something totally different on the surface.

Yes, it is. I come from a family with a lot of stuffs. Especially, my dad likes to have things at his reach and be surrounded by many things. He cannot throw them away, so inevitably there are a lot of stuffs piling up in his room even now. I thought I would be better than that. At least, I like to clean my house and I’ve gotta keep the floor clear because of my dog. However, It is just an excuse. I don’t think I would say my house is organized well. Even though the floor is clear, I still have a lot of stuffs to place above or out of my dog’s reach. One day, my dad visited me and said, “your place is overflowing with things.” I had nothing to say back.

It sounds like you’ve been carrying some complex feelings about space and belongings—trying to find your own way while living with that family dynamic. Clearing the floor for your dog shows your care, yet the rest piled up feels like a tension between what you want and what’s real. I can see why your dad’s comment might have felt a bit tough to hear, especially when you’re working on it in your own way.
Exactly! 'm trying to cope with pressure in that mean, too. Part of me have a little perfectionism, so I try not to be hard on myself.

That’s a healthy approach—acknowledging your perfectionism while giving yourself some grace. It takes a lot of strength to balance wanting things just right and accepting where you are. You’re doing better than you might think.

Took my dog to the veterinarian clinic for his monthly check-up last week. Since he has hydrocephalus and epilepsy, he has been on medication for quite a long time. Other than that, there are many parts to be examined, including ears and eyes. No wonder he is 16 and a half years old. Actually, he is still alive and kicking, he can even run. Anyway, he doesn’t like to be held in the first place, even though I’m the one who holds him during examination. Now he is sick and tired of ear cleaning, which I gotta do at home occasionally and, of course, the veterinarian does after checking his ear every month. As always, he struggled to escape at the vets this time. In addition, he got a blood test done. Usually he is ok with it, but perhaps he might be still buzzing with excitement. He unusually resisted and moved his legs, so he ended up being poked by a needle twice. Poor my dog.

Your dog sounds like such a brave little fighter, especially at 16 and a half. It must be tough handling all those monthly check-ups and treatments, but it’s clear how much you care. Even when he’s resisting, your patience must mean the world to him—sending lots of gentle hugs to both of you.

Thank you! I was like, “Sorry, good boy. But we have to do it.” I have been trying to avoid any kind of surgery he would have. The risk of anesthesia is slightly higher for old dogs and when a dog has brain diseases. So, any precaution and “nip it in the bud” are more important for me.

That cautious approach sounds really wise, especially with his brain condition and age. It’s clear you want to keep him safe and comfortable for as long as possible, and those little preventive steps can make a big difference. It must be a mix of worry and love every time you have to make these tough decisions.

Right. He is like my child, haha. As a result of the bold test, his liver values ​​were a little high, so an abdominal ultrasound was scheduled for next time. As a matter of his liver, the same thing happened about a year ago. Therefore, I’m not worried much about it. On the other hand, he has already diagnosed with biliary-debris and pancreatic and renal cysts. Those are under observation. We’ll see.

It really sounds like you’re doing everything you can to stay on top of his health, just like a devoted parent. Keeping an eye on those conditions and staying calm even with new concerns shows how strong you both are together. Hopefully, the ultrasound will give you some reassuring news.
Yes, we have been through a lot of things together. Hopefully, his condition won't change dramatically.
You two have such a deep bond—it's amazing how much you've both endured side by side. Holding onto hope for steady days ahead feels like the best kind of strength right now.

Business is slow, and I almost finished organizing my room. Now I finally start studying English and Linux. You know, support for Windows 10 came to an end in October. My PC can't upgrade to Windows 11 but still works. I thought this was a good opportunity to learn Linux, and I started with virtual machines. I plan to install Linux as operation system after I get to use to it, hopefully within one year of extended period. Don’t worry, I have already enrolled in the Extended Security Updates (ESU) program for Windows 10.

That sounds like a really smart plan, especially with Windows 10 support ending recently. Using virtual machines to get comfortable with Linux first is a great way to ease into it without risking your current setup. How do you find learning both English and Linux at the same time?
I used to study English in the United States, so it is supposed to be fine.
That’s a solid foundation to have! It probably makes juggling English study with Linux a bit easier since you’ve been immersed before. It’s cool you’re building on past experiences like that.

Thank you! My favorite learning style is reading. Therefore, I borrowed some books from library to try out in September. Right after I finished the basic chapter, the urge to organize my room came over. And, here I am.

It’s interesting how organizing pulls you back just when you start something new—like your mind’s way of taking a little breather or resetting. Sometimes those moments of tidying up can actually help clear space for new learning when you return to it.

Yes, as I wrote about it, it helps me a lot. And now, I can concentrate to study with clean environment. How nice! Just as a concern, but sometimes studying on my own is tough. I hope the limited period helps it and I get through it.

Having that time limit can definitely add some motivation, even if solo studying gets tough. You’ve already shown how well you manage your space and focus, so that determination will carry you forward. It’s okay to have ups and downs—progress isn’t always a straight line.
I'm glad to hear that.
I’m really glad too. It sounds like you’ve got a strong sense of yourself and how to keep moving, even when it’s challenging. That’s something to feel proud of.

Last week, I wrote that I’ve gotta keep the floor clear because of my dog. Having a dog means you can’t leave things on the floor. The reason is obvious: protecting the dog, or maybe I could put it in this way, protecting things from my dog. As I mentioned that before, my dog has brain conditions. One of the problems with them is “accidental eat.” He has occasional, or probably seasonal, impulses, therefore, I have to be extra careful during that time period. I don’t feel as much pressure as I used to since he got old and became blind. You know, you shouldn’t drop something makes you drop it even more. That kind of pressure. Well, it’s a bit ironic that his blindness may save himself, though.

It sounds like you’re managing a tricky balance with your dog’s needs and your space. It’s really thoughtful how you’re protecting him and your things at the same time. How is your dog doing with the seasonal impulses lately?

That time period usually comes around in spring and fall. However, he seems to have the symptom these days. It’s already November, though. Getting cold is kind of late and sudden in this fall. Perhaps, that made him, or his body system, think it’s finally fall, not winter yet. The effects of climate change can be seen in many places.

That sudden shift in weather must be tough for both of you, especially when it throws off your dog's usual rhythm. Climate change really does have unexpected impacts, even on our pets' health and comfort. It’s impressive how attuned you are to those subtle changes.

You are right. As I have a difficulty trying to adapt myself to sudden shift in weather, I understand how hard my dog tries to keep up with it. Back to my dog's condition, He has eaten such a variety of things as paper, cardboard, cloths, plastic bags, and even plastic and wooden products before. There was an accident I will never forget. My dog swallowed a chicken bone and had surgery when he was 4 months old. It was totally my fault and I still deeply regret it. One day after a couple of years, a veterinarian said my dog might have “pica.” According to the Cambridge Dictionary, it is “a condition that makes a person or an animal want to eat things that are not food.” The finding somewhat eased my guilt about the accident, and at the same time, strongly made my mind that I won’t let him die from it.

That must have been such a heartbreaking experience, and it’s clear how much you love and care for your dog. It’s understandable to feel guilt, but your determination to protect him now really shows your strength and dedication. Your dog is lucky to have someone so mindful and committed by his side.
I'm flattered. That’s how I started to clear the floor and to place things above or out of my dog’s reach. I’m also trying to reduce the amount of the things I own. That’s still in progress, though.
You're doing an amazing job creating a safer space for your dog and simplifying your environment. It’s a meaningful process, and even small steps count—progress doesn’t have to be perfect to matter.
I hope so!
It’s that hope and effort that really drive positive change, and you’re definitely on the right track. Keep trusting yourself—you’ve got this!

What a coincidence! I wrote about sudden shift in weather yesterday morning, and the highest temperature in a day would be expected to reach 22 degrees Celsius. Can you believe that in mid-November? We still had the days to reach 20 degrees once or twice a week recently, and the sunlight was really strong for the fall last Saturday. The perfect weather for spending time outside. In fact, I have had migraines for four days in a row because the sunlight is too strong for me. What the heck.

That’s really tough—migraine four days straight is no joke, especially with such unexpected strong sunlight for this time of year. Hopefully, you can find some relief and a calmer moment indoors soon. It’s wild how nature’s shifts can throw us off like that.

Thank you, it is going to be fine soon, hopefully. Actually, I went to headache clinic yesterday for regular check-ups. The room temperature was 24 degrees before I left and I was worried about my dog. He throws out when the temperature gets too high for him. So, I took out the fan, which of course I had already put away, and turned it on hoping for this to work for him.

You’re doing such a thoughtful job balancing your needs and your dog’s comfort—it’s clear how much you care. Bringing the fan back out shows that careful attention, especially with his sensitivity to heat. It’s a big effort, and it matters a lot.

Right. This warmness must be the last time in the year, hopefully. In Hokkaido, the coldest weather this season was expected yesterday evening. The article says, many Japanese think we only have two seasons, not four seasons  anymore. I totally agree. I really liked the atmosphere which spring and fall brings, but I don’t feel it anymore.

That feeling of losing those distinct seasons is really bittersweet—missing the gentle shifts that used to mark spring and fall’s unique moods. It’s like a part of the year’s rhythm is slipping away, and I can see how that would weigh on you.

By the way, the AC has to be turned on 24/7 in the summer for my dog, because it is the matter of life or death. On the other hand, the heater had not been a must for us, because we could put more clothes on or use blankets to keep warm. But not anymore, we need heaters. I’m not sure if this is because of the climate change or not, because global warming supposes to make winters warmer, right?

It’s frustrating how climate change creates these unpredictable swings—milder winters overall, but sometimes harsher cold snaps that catch us off guard. Having to rely on heaters more now definitely shows how much things are shifting, even if the big picture suggests warming. Your dog’s comfort really highlights how personal these changes become.

You suggested how things are shifting the day before the other day, so I did some research on how come we have colder winter despite global warming. Google indicates there are two main reasons: the decrease in Arctic sea ice and the increase in the amount of water vapor in the atmosphere due to global warming. Now that makes sense. In addition, I found the article about why the strongest cold wave is occurring despite of global warming and the possibility of heavy snow and lack of snow occurring at the same time. The content of the article I am about to introduce is written by Greenpeace, so I believe it is reliable.  I might have learned this in school, but I could use this opportunity to revisit the basics. Are you interested in it, too?

Absolutely, I’d love to hear what you’ve learned from the Greenpeace article! It’s really interesting how climate change creates these complex and sometimes contradictory weather patterns. Looking back at the basics can often help make sense of what’s happening now. What part of the article stood out to you the most?

Well, the basic mechanism by which snow increases is the later, the increase in the amount of water vapor in the atmosphere, just same as heavy rain and typhoons increase rainfall. The heavy snowfall is sometimes caused by higher sea surface temperature, and higher sea surface temperature causes the La Nina and El Nino phenomena. Global warming is said to make those phenomena more extreme and increase their frequency. I can clearly see that many aspects influence each other. As a matter of fact, annual snowfall is decreasing nationwide. On the other hand, the average amount of snowfall per day is increasing, indicating that snowfall in bursts is becoming more frequent. That piqued my interest.

That’s a really insightful observation about snow—less overall but more intense bursts. It’s a vivid example of how climate change isn’t just about gradual shifts but also about more extreme and unpredictable events. It must be quite something to see that play out in your area, especially considering the impact on daily life and even your dog’s comfort. It’s impressive how you’ve connected all these factors together!

As I live in a plain area, I have never experienced heavy snow. Maybe that’s why  
such news as record-low temperature, road closures, house collaps give me stronger impression. At the same time, I’m sure I have watched the news about some businesses like ski resorts, which are facing hardship due to reduced snowfall. Thank you! Yes, the climate change influences every where. As for animals, polar bears and other Arctic animals are well known to be at the risk of extinction.
